items.title: Known limits
items.text:
• Overhead is large. f_trace_opcodes fires per instruction, and this is not the mechanism for production runs; sys.monitoring with only BRANCH and CALL enabled is.
  • Only one trace function and one profile function can be installed per thread, so this conflicts with debuggers, coverage and profilers. Say so in the docstring rather than trying to chain them.
  • Threads need threading.settrace separately; not handled here.
  • coverage.py was evaluated for this and rejected, because CoverageData does not store the called lines in order. Recorded so nobody re-evaluates it.

items.title: M12 awl.editor implementation plan
items.text:
For agentic workers: REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task.

Goal: The editing model, headless. What nodes may be placed, what an edit does to the document, and whether the result is still a legal workflow.

Architecture: Pure functions over CompactDoc. No browser, no rendering. Every edit returns a new document and an edit list M10 can apply to source by span, so the visual and textual representations never diverge.

Tech Stack: Python stdlib plus jsonschema.

items.title: Contract
items.text: Consumes CompactDoc, a workflow domain JSON Schema Produces CompactDoc plus an edit list Depends on awl.contracts, awl.compact

items.title: The palette has two sources, and needs both
items.text:
Source Supplies Mechanism The workflow domain schema which constructs and callees are legal plain JSON Schema enum constraints The OO-LD class schemas the typed parameter form for each entry the same generator that produces forms and pydantic classes

The first alone gives a list of names. The second is what makes the claim non-obvious: a ChargeParam entry that already knows its fields, their ranges and their widgets, because Diameter.schema.json and its siblings in oold-reference-schemas carry that. Blockly needs a hand-written block definition per construct and React Flow a hand-written node component; here both fall out of schemas that already exist.

An earlier draft did only the first and described it as "derived from the OO-LD schema", which was a narrowing presented as the full claim.

items.title: Legality: plain JSON Schema, no new keywords
items.text:
This is the part with no precedent. Blockly requires a hand-written block definition per construct; React Flow requires a hand-written node component. Here the available node types fall out of the schema that already generates forms and pydantic classes.

No new keywords. An earlier draft of this spec invented x-awl-constructs and x-awl-callees. That was wrong, for a reason worth recording so it is not reinvented: an AWL document is the AST as JSON, so ordinary JSON Schema already expresses the restriction, which is what the awl-schema README states as objective 3, "allow only a whitelist of function calls".

{
  "$defs": {
    "node": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "_type":  {"enum": ["Module", "FunctionDef", "If", "While", "Call"]},
        "callee": {"enum": ["battery.device.charge", "battery.device.rest"]}
      }
    }
  },
  "$ref": "#/$defs/node"
}

Verified against this schema:

Document Result {"_type": "Call", "callee": "battery.device.charge"} accepted {"_type": "Call", "callee": "os.system"} rejected {"_type": "ClassDef"} rejected

Two reasons the plain-schema form is strictly better than a vendor keyword:

  • Any standard validator enforces it. With x-awl-callees, only AWL-aware code would know the rule; a generic validator must ignore unknown keywords and would pass os.system. That inverts the restriction objective, turning a constraint into a hint.
  • One artefact, not two. A schema carrying both a keyword list and its own properties encodes the same constraint twice, which is the drift problem OO-LD exists to eliminate.

items.title: Edits return a patch, not just a document
items.text: An edit that only returned the new document would force the writer to diff two trees and guess which source range changed. Returning the span makes M10's job mechanical and keeps the round trip exact.

items.title: Non-goals
items.text:
• Not rendering. That is M13.
  • Not source patching. That is M10; this produces the instruction, not the result.

"""The headless editing model: palette, edits, and domain validation."""

from __future__ import annotations

import copy
from typing import Any

__all__ = ["palette", "set_literal", "validate_domain"]

# Properties whose enum constraints define what may be placed. Extending this
# is a deliberate change: each entry is a claim about what a domain profile
# is allowed to restrict.
_PALETTE_SOURCES = (("_type", "construct"), ("callee", "callee"))


def _collect_enum(node: Any, prop: str, out: list[str]) -> None:
    """Gather enum values for *prop* anywhere in the schema, including $defs."""
    if isinstance(node, list):
        for item in node:
            _collect_enum(item, prop, out)
    elif isinstance(node, dict):
        properties = node.get("properties")
        if isinstance(properties, dict) and isinstance(properties.get(prop), dict):
            values = properties[prop].get("enum")
            if isinstance(values, list):
                out.extend(values)
        for value in node.values():
            _collect_enum(value, prop, out)


def palette(schema: dict[str, Any]) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    """Derive the placeable node types from a workflow domain schema.

    Reads ordinary JSON Schema ``enum`` constraints. There is no AWL-specific
    keyword, so the same schema both drives the palette and is enforced by any
    standard validator.

    Parameters
    ----------
    schema : dict
        A workflow domain JSON Schema.

    Returns
    -------
    list of dict
        Each has ``name`` and ``kind``, deduplicated, in schema order. Empty
        when the schema declares no enum, which means the domain permits
        nothing rather than everything.
    """
    seen: set[tuple[str, str]] = set()
    entries: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    for prop, kind in _PALETTE_SOURCES:
        found: list[str] = []
        _collect_enum(schema, prop, found)
        for name in found:
            if (kind, name) not in seen:
                seen.add((kind, name))
                entries.append({"name": name, "kind": kind})
    return entries

def test_setting_a_literal_returns_both_the_document_and_the_span():
    """The fixture is a real CompactDoc, produced by M9, not hand-shaped.

    An earlier draft used an invented path that does not occur in any encoded
    document, so the addressing model was never exercised. The real shape of
    `charge(ChargeParam(target_voltage=4.2))` nests Expr, Call, args, Call,
    keywords, and the path below is measured from it.
    """
    import ast

    from ast2json import ast2json

    from awl.compact import encode

    doc = encode(ast2json(ast.parse("charge(ChargeParam(target_voltage=4.2))\n")))
    path = ["body", 0, "value", "args", 0, "keywords", 0, "value"]

    probe = doc
    for key in path:
        probe = probe[key]
    assert probe == {"c": 4.2}, "the path is real"

    new_doc, edits = set_literal(doc, path=path, value=4.1, span={"start": 35, "end": 38})

    probe = new_doc
    for key in path:
        probe = probe[key]
    assert probe == {"c": 4.1}
    assert edits == [{"start": 35, "end": 38, "text": "4.1"}]

    probe = doc
    for key in path:
        probe = probe[key]
    assert probe == {"c": 4.2}, "the input is not mutated"
  • [ ] Step 2: Implement
def set_literal(
    doc: dict[str, Any], *, path: list[Any], value: Any, span: dict[str, int]
) -> tuple[dict[str, Any], list[dict[str, Any]]]:
    """Replace a literal, returning the new document and a source patch.

    Returning the patch is what keeps the visual and textual representations
    from diverging: M10 applies it by span rather than regenerating the file.
    """
    out = copy.deepcopy(doc)
    target = out
    for key in path[:-1]:
        target = target[key]
    target[path[-1]] = {"c": value}
    return out, [{"start": span["start"], "end": span["end"], "text": repr(value)}]
  • [ ] Step 3: Run and commit
git commit -am "feat(editor): edits return a document and a source patch"

    assert [s["order"] for s in new_doc["body"]] == [0, 1], "order is renumbered"

        {"_": "Call", "$callee": "charge", "order": 0},

    assert new_doc["body"][0]["$callee"] == "rest"


def test_reordering_updates_order_not_just_position():
    """order is the query surface. A reorder that moves list position without
    updating order would leave the RDF saying the opposite of the document.
    """
    doc = {"_": "Module", "body": [
        {"_": "Call", "$callee": "charge", "order": 0},
        {"_": "Call", "$callee": "rest", "order": 1},

items.text:
• [ ] The palette contains exactly what the schema's enums permit, deduplicated, found through $defs nesting.
  • [ ] A schema declaring nothing yields an empty palette, not an unrestricted one.
  • [ ] An edit returns a new document plus a span patch, and does not mutate its input.

items.title: Known limits
items.text:
• Palette derivation requires the restriction to be written as enum. not, allOf and oneOf combinations are equally valid JSON Schema and equally enforced, but they are not enumerable, so a domain profile using them validates correctly while offering an empty palette. That is a documented convention for domain profiles, not a code fix: do not try to invert arbitrary schema algebra.
  • _PALETTE_SOURCES fixes which properties drive the palette. Adding one is a deliberate change, because each entry asserts something about what a domain profile may restrict.
  • Structural edits (add, delete, reorder) produce patches M10 can only apply via libcst. Keep them behind the same API so M13 never needs to know which tier applies.

items.title: M13 awl.ui implementation plan
items.text:
For agentic workers: REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task.

Goal: Render a workflow, let a human edit it, write the result back to source, and overlay what actually ran.

Architecture: An anywidget component, so one artefact serves the notebook, a Panel app via AnyWidgetComponent, and JupyterLite. Two variants are built and compared, because the canvas paradigm is the same decision as whether control flow is the differentiator, and it should be settled by evidence.

Tech Stack: anywidget, jedison or RJSF, Blockly or React Flow, Cytoscape.js. pytest-playwright for tests.

items.title: Contract
items.text: Consumes CompactDoc from M12, TraceEvent list from M11 Produces rendered UI, and edit lists routed back through M12 Depends on awl.editor, awl.trace, awl.contracts

items.title: The paradigm decision
items.text:
Node-graph editors model dataflow. Block editors model control flow. AWL-LD's differentiator against CWL, PWD and semantikon is that it carries if and while. React Flow makes a nested loop body awkward, needing group nodes or subflow conventions; Blockly represents nested statements natively with C-shaped blocks and already ships a Python generator.

Choosing a node-graph canvas quietly pushes the model back toward the dataflow shape the ecosystem already occupies. That is a product decision, so build both and measure.

Variant Canvas Form Notes A control-flow-first Blockly jedison No React anywhere. Native nested statements B dataflow-first React Flow RJSF RJSF is the path of least resistance in React

Both consume the same M12 model, so the comparison isolates the paradigm rather than the plumbing.

Criteria, fixed before building so the result is not rationalised afterwards:

  1. How a nested while body reads.
  2. How a typed parameter form fits inside a node.
  3. How a trace overlay attaches to the same nodes.
  4. Bundle size under JupyterLite.

items.title: Form library: jedison over RJSF, for a principle reason
items.text:
jedison 1.19.0 react-jsonschema-form Runtime dependencies zero React, @rjsf/validator-ajv8 (ajv), a theme Drafts explicit modules for 04, 06, 07, 2019-09, 2020-12 via ajv8 Conformance testing official json-schema-test-suite in devDeps ajv's $ref own ref-parser via ajv Widget selection x-format, inside the schema uiSchema, a separate object

The decisive argument is a principle argument. RJSF's uiSchema is a second artefact, and OO-LD exists because keeping structure and semantics in two files makes them drift. jedison's x-format lives in the schema, the same in-schema extension pattern as x-oold-*, and applyOverlay supports the layered approach when it is wanted deliberately.

Two supporting points: this project is already on that codebase (OoldEditor imports @json-editor/json-editor, and jedison's author has 601 commits on json-editor against the original author's 315), and zero dependencies matters for the JupyterLite target the HITL example names.

RJSF wins on React Flow embedding, since jedison is imperative DOM and needs a mount and unmount wrapper that survives React 18 StrictMode double-invocation.

Not yet verified: that @context and x-oold-* pass through jedison untouched. Both specifications require unknown keywords to be ignored and json-editor already handles these schemas, so the risk is low, but test it against a real OO-LD schema before committing.

items.text:
• Not the editing model. That is M12, and it is testable without a browser.
  • Not graph analysis. Cytoscape.js provides a read-only view of the RDF and trace graphs; do not make one library do both jobs.

"""Visual workflow editor, delivered as an anywidget."""

from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

import anywidget
import traitlets

_STATIC = Path(__file__).parent / "static"


class WorkflowEditor(anywidget.AnyWidget):
    """Render and edit a workflow, and overlay a trace.

    One component serves the notebook, Panel via AnyWidgetComponent, and
    JupyterLite, because all three consume plain ESM.
    """

    document = traitlets.Dict().tag(sync=True)
    trace_events = traitlets.List().tag(sync=True)
    variant = traitlets.Unicode("a").tag(sync=True)

    @property
    def _esm(self) -> str:
        return (_STATIC / f"variant_{self.variant}.js").read_text(encoding="utf-8")

items.title: M14 awl.pipeline implementation plan
items.text:
For agentic workers: REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task.

Goal: Compose the modules, and prove the composition actually works.

Architecture: pipeline.py holds no logic of its own. It is the one place allowed to import several modules, so every testable behaviour stays in a module that can be verified alone. The value of this spec is not the code; it is the integration tests, which cover the failure class no per-module test can reach.

Tech Stack: Everything. This is the only module that depends on more than awl.contracts.

items.title: Why this exists
items.text:
The architecture is deliberately contract-isolated: a module depends on another module's data contract, never its code. That buys parallel implementation, and it buys one specific blind spot.

Contracts guarantee that shapes line up. They guarantee nothing about meaning. Thirteen modules can each pass their own suite, every document can validate against its schema, and the pipeline can still be wrong, because:

  • M3 mints an identity for ChargeParam, M6 looks up a different one, and the collapse silently never fires. Both modules pass.
  • M4 marks a binding AMBIGUOUS, M6 collapses it anyway, and retrofitted meaning becomes indistinguishable from declared meaning. Both modules pass.
  • M5 elides a node M9's decoder needs, and the ast profile stops round-tripping. Both modules pass.

Every one of those is an integration failure with green unit tests. That is what this module owns.

items.title: Contract
items.text: Consumes source text, a profile name, a domain schema Produces AstDoc, quads, or a CompactDoc, depending on the entry point Depends on all modules

items.title: Non-goals
items.text:
• Not a place for logic. If a test here fails and the fix is code in pipeline.py, the fix is in the wrong module. Push it down and give it a unit test.
  • Not a replacement for module suites. It is the composition check, not the correctness check.

from awl.pipeline import to_rdf

SOURCE = (contracts.CORPUS_DIR / "tier3_oold" / "procedure.py").read_text(encoding="utf-8")

"""Compose the modules. No behaviour of its own lives here."""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any

from awl import collapse, context, elide, facts, rdf, resolve

__all__ = ["to_ast_doc", "to_rdf"]


def to_ast_doc(source: str, *, module: str, profile: str = "workflow") -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Run source through extraction, resolution, elision and collapse."""
    import ast

    from ast2json import ast2json

    observed = facts.extract(source, module=module)
    bound = resolve.resolve(observed)
    types = {t["identity"]["symbol"]: t for t in observed["types"]}
    resolved = {
        b["localName"]: b["identity"]["symbol"]
        for b in bound["bindings"]
        if b["confidence"] == "EXTRACTED" and "identity" in b
    }

    doc = ast2json(ast.parse(source))
    # `source` is threaded through so opaque nodes keep their expression text.
    doc = elide.elide(doc, profile=profile, source=source)
    return collapse.collapse(doc, types=types, resolved=resolved)


def to_rdf(source: str, *, module: str, profile: str = "workflow"):
    """Run the full chain and return an rdflib Graph.

    The extracted types are passed into the context builder, so numeric field
    annotations become explicit xsd:double coercions. Omitting them silently
    drops the cross-language numeric mitigation.
    """
    observed = facts.extract(source, module=module)
    doc = to_ast_doc(source, module=module, profile=profile)
    return rdf.to_graph(doc, context=context.build_context(observed["types"]))


def to_compact(source: str, *, module: str, profile: str = "ast", spans: bool = True):
    """Run the chain and return the editor model.

    M9 consumes an AstDoc, which is what M5 emits, so the two compose. Spans
    default on here because the editor needs them as a join key.
    """
    from awl import compact

    return compact.encode(to_ast_doc(source, module=module, profile=profile), keep_spans=spans)

items.title: Task 2: Producers agree on identity
items.text:
The most valuable test in the suite, because it is the exact failure graphify/ids.py documents and no unit test can see it.

  • [ ] Step 1: Write the test
def test_every_producer_mints_the_same_identity_for_one_entity():
    """Three producers, one entity. If they disagree the graph silently splits.

    graphify/ids.py: "Three independent producers must agree on node IDs or
    the graph splits a single entity into disconnected ghost nodes." Here it
    is worse than in graphify, because these are global IRIs: a disagreement
    is a wrong assertion about the world, not a local inconsistency.
    """
    source = (contracts.CORPUS_DIR / "tier3_oold" / "params.py").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    observed = facts.extract(source, module="tier3_oold.params")

    from_facts = {t["identity"]["iri"] for t in observed["types"]}

    doc = to_ast_doc(
        (contracts.CORPUS_DIR / "tier3_oold" / "procedure.py").read_text(encoding="utf-8"),
        module="tier3_oold.procedure",
    )
    from_collapse = _collect_types(doc)

    graph = to_rdf(source, module="tier3_oold.params")
    from_rdf = {str(o) for _, p, o in graph if str(p).endswith("type")}

    assert from_collapse <= from_facts, f"collapse invented {from_collapse - from_facts}"
    assert from_rdf <= from_facts, f"rdf invented {from_rdf - from_facts}"


def _collect_types(doc):
    found = set()
    if isinstance(doc, dict):
        if "@type" in doc:
            found.add(doc["@type"])
        for value in doc.values():
            found |= _collect_types(value)
    elif isinstance(doc, list):
        for item in doc:
            found |= _collect_types(item)
    return found
  • [ ] Step 2: Run and commit
git commit -am "test(pipeline): pin identity agreement across producers"

def test_an_ambiguous_binding_is_never_collapsed():
    """M4 says AMBIGUOUS, M6 must not collapse anyway.

    A star import is used deliberately: a plain `from x import Y` resolves
    EXTRACTED, so an earlier version of this test exercised the unknown-type
    path and never touched ambiguity at all.
    """
    source = "from mystery import *\nUnknown(a=1)\n"
    facts = __import__("awl.facts", fromlist=["extract"]).extract(source, module="scratch")
    bound = __import__("awl.resolve", fromlist=["resolve"]).resolve(facts)
    tiers = {b["confidence"] for b in bound["bindings"]}
    assert "AMBIGUOUS" in tiers, "the fixture must actually produce ambiguity"

    doc = to_ast_doc(source, module="scratch")
    assert _collect_types(doc) == set(), "an ambiguous callee must stay a Call"


def test_an_unknown_type_is_also_not_collapsed():
    """The other path, kept separate so neither masks the other."""
    doc = to_ast_doc("from mystery import Unknown\nUnknown(a=1)\n", module="scratch")
    assert _collect_types(doc) == set()

These are the four end-to-end claims. Each is a promise made in the analysis, so each gets a test rather than a note.

import ast

import pytest


@pytest.mark.parametrize("path", contracts.corpus_files(), ids=lambda p: f"{p.parent.name}/{p.name}")
def test_the_ast_profile_round_trips(path):
    from json2ast import json2ast

    source = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    doc = to_ast_doc(source, module=path.stem, profile="ast")
    restored = json2ast(doc)
    assert ast.unparse(ast.fix_missing_locations(restored)) == ast.unparse(ast.parse(source))


def test_the_workflow_profile_answers_the_ordering_question():
    """The concrete measure of success: impossible with the current code.

    Which charge steps precede a rest step, and at what target voltage.
    """
    graph = to_rdf(
        (contracts.CORPUS_DIR / "tier3_oold" / "procedure.py").read_text(encoding="utf-8"),
        module="tier3_oold.procedure",
    )
    rows = list(graph.query("""
        PREFIX awl: <https://w3id.org/awl/schema/>
        SELECT ?voltage WHERE {
            ?step awl:index ?i ;
                  awl:hasArgument [ awl:target_voltage ?voltage ] .
        } ORDER BY ?i
    """))
    assert rows, "statement order and the collapsed argument are both reachable"


def test_a_float_survives_the_rdf_round_trip():
    """4.0 must not come back as an integer.

    The coercion is derived from the field annotations M3 reads, so the
    pipeline must pass the extracted types into build_context(). An earlier
    version called build_context() with no arguments, which installs no
    coercion term at all and made this assertion structurally undemonstrable.
    """
    from rdflib import XSD

    source = (contracts.CORPUS_DIR / "tier3_oold" / "procedure.py").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    graph = to_rdf(source, module="tier3_oold.procedure")
    doubles = [o for _, _, o in graph if getattr(o, "datatype", None) == XSD.double]
    assert doubles, "a float-annotated field produced an xsd:double coercion"


def test_statement_order_needs_no_list_traversal():
    """@list gives fidelity; the materialized index gives queryability."""
    graph = to_rdf(
        (contracts.CORPUS_DIR / "tier2_dataclass" / "procedure.py").read_text(encoding="utf-8"),
        module="tier2_dataclass.procedure",
    )
    indices = [int(o) for _, p, o in graph if str(p).endswith("index")]
    assert indices == sorted(indices) and len(indices) > 1

items.title: Acceptance
items.text:
• [ ] The chain runs source to RDF without a module knowing about another module's code.
  • [ ] All producers mint the same identity for one entity.
  • [ ] An AMBIGUOUS binding is never collapsed.
  • [ ] Every corpus file round-trips at the ast profile, including the vendored real-world sample.
  • [ ] The ordering query returns rows.
  • [ ] A float stays xsd:double.
  • [ ] Statement order is readable from an integer index without list traversal.
  • [ ] pipeline.py contains no branching logic of its own.

items.title: Known limits
items.text:
• These tests are slow relative to unit tests, because each runs the whole chain. Mark them so make test can exclude them during tight iteration, but never exclude them from make ci.
  • A failure here is often ambiguous about which module is at fault. That is inherent to integration testing; resist the urge to add diagnostics to pipeline.py, and instead add the missing unit test to whichever module the investigation implicates.
  • The real-world corpus file is roughly half matplotlib plotting. If the ambient-vocabulary filter is too aggressive it will strip meaningful calls too; if too lax the graph fills with plotting noise. That tension is best observed here, on real code, rather than on a hand-written fixture.
